I'm 49 years old and I've been farming in Quzhou County my whole life. The land here is flat, the soil is loamy, and if you manage it right, you can get two crops in one year. I don't have much schooling, but I know these fields. Every year, I plant winter wheat after the National Day holiday in October, and I harvest it in early June. The very next day, I put in summer maize. There's no time to rest between them—you lose a day, you lose yield. The grain station takes wheat, and traders come to the village for maize, so I know I can sell them.

I buy my wheat seed from the county seed station—improved varieties like Jimai or Luneng series that resist lodging and do well here. For maize, I only plant hybrid seed, usually from Zhengdan or Xianyu lines; the seed costs more but the yield difference pays for itself. I apply compound fertilizer as a base and then top-dress with urea when the crops need it most—jointing stage for wheat, and the big喇叭口 stage for maize. I irrigate three times for each crop: my wells still pump, and I can't rely on the rain alone in Hebei. I spray herbicide once and then fungicide or insecticide once more if I see pests or disease. I till with the rotary tiller; it's fast and good enough for these soils. I expect about 550 kg per mu from the wheat and 650 kg per mu from the maize if the weather is fair.
